data.title: ‘Like a father to me’: Hong Kong bids farewell to Tung Chee-hwa in weekend vigil
data.description:
Tung Chee-hwa became Hong Kong’s first chief executive after its return to Chinese rule in 1997, before stepping down in 2005, citing health reasons.
During his tenure, Hong Kong was hit by the Asian financial crisis in 1998 and a Sars outbreak in 2003. Tung also attempted to enact national security legislation to fulfil the provisions under Article 23 of the Basic Law, the city’s mini-constitution. The bill was later shelved after half a million residents took to the streets to oppose the move.
Tung was later appointed as a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top advisory body.

data.title: Hong Kong leader says firms must strive to survive despite government support
data.description:
Hong Kong’s leader defended measures in his policy address to boost the economy and improve livelihoods, stressing that businesses must also do their part to remain competitive and survive, even with government aid.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Saturday that the livelihood section was the longest and broadest in scope in his policy address when asked about residents who had yet to benefit from the government’s economic policies.
“You need to develop the economy first to have the resources to improve people’s livelihoods,” Lee said on a radio programme discussing his policy address and Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, which he announced on Wednesday.
“First, we must grow the overall economy so that everyone benefits, but as the pie grows bigger, there are indeed certain groups that may need extra help.”
He pointed to funding for small and medium-sized enterprises to help them expand into more markets, develop e-commerce and enhance their capabilities through technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI).
But Lee said that, in a survival-of-the-fittest society, effort was needed from “both sides”.
“While the government works hard, business operators might also need to think of ways themselves because, after all, this is a highly competitive society,” he said.
“Individuals still need to make their own efforts to improve themselves.”
He said the government would assist businesses by providing funding, expanding their potential markets and encouraging them to “think about what the world values right now”.
In his policy address, Lee announced 10 measures to support the development, upgrading and transformation of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

These include the Hong Kong Export Credit Insurance Corporation extending its offer of 20 free buyer credit checks for another year, until September 2027, to continue supporting its insured markets.
However, Eric Ho, 44, owner of Sai Wah restaurant in Wan Chai, told the South China Morning Post that he was still struggling to survive after he and his partner spent HK$6 million (US$764,778) setting up the business in 2023, following the Covid-19 pandemic.
“At that time we were all upbeat about opening up Hong Kong to the world so we splashed the money on the restaurant. We all thought that there would be an economic revival,” he said.
Despite its roughly 70 seats and workforce of more than a dozen people, Ho soon found that the growing trend of Hongkongers crossing the border to spend was taking a toll on the restaurant’s business.
“During weekends, local diners also disappeared. Apparently, they all went north to spend and consume on the mainland,” he said.
Ho also blamed a lack of tourists for the business’s difficulties.
“The external environment is really not good. Our operating cost is high, including staff wages, food costs and the consistent rent hike,” he said.
“The wage of imported labour is higher than that of local staff, posing a burden on us.”

Ho hoped the government would introduce measures to attract more overseas visitors and stabilise the imported labour scheme so wages could be kept at market rates rather than aligned with the median monthly wage of local workers.
In his policy address, Lee also referred to chapters on improving urban management and addressing traffic and water-pipe problems, saying such measures were relevant to residents’ well-being.
“When we talk about livelihood welfare, we hope there are no burst water pipes, our traffic remains smooth, and our overall urban management is improved,” he said.
“We don’t want sudden power outages, nor do we want severe traffic congestion. All of these belong to public welfare.”
Asked how authorities would restore public confidence after the Wang Fuk Court fire, Lee pledged systematic reforms and said his policy address had outlined several priority measures.
“But I can firmly tell you that is not all of the measures,” he said.
“After the Independent Commission submits its report in October, the recommendations will be actively followed up to launch more comprehensive reforms addressing all issues at once.”
Additional reporting by Cannix Yau

data.title: Patriot dedicated to Hong Kong: business heavyweights remember Tung Chee-hwa
data.description:
This weekend, Hong Kong mourns the loss of former chief executive and elder statesman Tung Chee-hwa.
The shipping tycoon who became the city’s first leader after its transfer of sovereignty to China in 1997 died on September 8 at the age of 89, leaving a legacy of determined stewardship and dedicated public service.
This weekend, a state funeral will be held to honour Tung, who was also a former vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). There will be a vigil on Saturday and a memorial on Sunday, while condolence books will be opened for the public at multiple venues from Friday to Sunday.

The South China Morning Post is running a special commemorative print supplement on Saturday, sharing reflections from those who knew Tung personally.
Join us for part two, featuring tributes from business heavyweights. Read part one here. You can also find other tributes from the supplement here and here.

Joe Tsai, chairman of Alibaba Group
I am deeply saddened by the passing of Mr Tung Chee-hwa. He was affectionately known to me and my family as “Uncle CH” because of our common Zhejiang roots and friendship from my parents’ generation.
As founder of the China-United States Exchange Foundation, Mr Tung worked tirelessly to build trust, understanding and friendship between China and the United States. I have personally witnessed his dedication to this mission, even in his late years, as he braved long flights travelling to the United States to engage in dialogue with his friends and interlocutors in America.

He would call me to his office and urge me to build more bridges between the peoples of the two countries. I am grateful to him as a mentor and, most importantly, he set an example for all of us as a man of honour, integrity, loyalty and leadership.
Mr Tung’s wholehearted devotion and his lifelong commitment to serving the best interests of our nation will be remembered with enduring respect.
Mr Tung served as an independent director of Alibaba Group for eight years since Alibaba’s IPO in September 2014. We as a company pay tribute to him and thank him for his invaluable contribution and unwavering support.

Robert Ng Chee Siong, former chairman of Sino Group
Mr Tung consistently highlighted the global significance of stable Sino-US relations.
He invited me to his home on many occasions and facilitated dialogue between visiting US members of Congress and mainland officials, building bridges for mutual understanding.
Mr Tung worked tirelessly for Hong Kong’s stability and prosperity, and never wavered from this goal.
A true patriot dedicated to Hong Kong, his foresight, sincerity and unwavering devotion leave a lasting legacy.
We will always remember him.

Peter Woo Kwong-ching
Mr Tung Chee-hwa was a man with a big heart, and a lifelong patriot.
In 1996, CH and I ran for the first chief executive election. It was a gentlemen’s contest and we were united by the common goal of contributing to the better development and start of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
As the elected chief executive, Mr Tung appointed me as chairman of the Trade Development Council, a role I accepted with honour.
As the first chief executive, Mr Tung contributed immensely to the government’s implementation of “one country, two systems” with tireless dedication. His accomplishments stand as a legacy and his noble spirit will continue to be a guiding force for generations to come.
CH continued after his years as chief executive with non-stop initiatives, both internationally and in Hong Kong, that were highly effective and with meaningful outcomes.
CH and I were once neighbours and we were also together in the shipping industry in the early days.
He was a dear friend and an outstanding leader, and he will be dearly missed.
Woo was previously chairman of Wheelock Holdings and The Wharf. He wrote the tribute in his personal capacity.

Annie Wu Suk-ching, lifetime honorary board member, World Trade Centres Association
I first met the late Mr Tung Chee-hwa when he campaigned for the post of Hong Kong chief executive. Ever since, he has given great support to NGO projects aimed at nurturing patriotism and a commitment to serve Hong Kong in the younger generation.
The most memorable NGO project was the Chinese History, Culture and Education Foundation for Youth, set up in 1998.
Not only did Mr Tung become the foundation’s honorary patron - with honorary advisers including the head of New China News Agency and commissioner of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs - he also personally attended major occasions and ceremonies to hand out flags to the participants of study tours from 1998 to 2003.
The NGO carried out 120 educational visits to many major Chinese cities in the provinces. His dedication has inspired students, teachers and principals alike. They were greatly impressed watching the flag-raising ceremony in Tiananmen Square at 3am and meeting government leaders in the Great Hall of the People.
Many of them were deeply impressed by Mr Tung’s vision and passion, and have since then served Hong Kong remembering his words: “If Hong Kong is good, China will be good. If China is good, Hong Kong will be even better.”

data.title: Friend, leader, mentor: how political veterans remember Tung Chee-hwa
data.description:
This weekend, Hong Kong mourns the loss of former chief executive and elder statesman Tung Chee-hwa.
The shipping tycoon who became the city’s first leader after its transfer of sovereignty to China in 1997 died on September 8 at the age of 89, leaving a legacy of determined stewardship and dedicated public service.
He is remembered for steering Hong Kong through uncharted waters following the end of colonial rule, as well as his tireless efforts as a state leader and business heavyweight to help repair, maintain and improve Sino-US relations.

Tributes have been pouring in locally and from overseas to reflect the high regard in which he was held, many remembering him as a wise, kind and exceptionally hard-working leader with a deep love for Hong Kong and the country.
He was a pioneering steward of the unprecedented “one country, two systems” experiment, the governing formula for Hong Kong that he oversaw in its initial application and supported in its continuing success.
Tung’s tenure from 1997 to 2005 as chief executive was tested by a series of major challenges, from the Asian financial crisis and the deadly Sars epidemic to mass protests over national security legislation.


He stumbled at times, drawing criticism, but was unwavering in his commitment to Hong Kong’s stability and prosperity, and initiated policies that laid the groundwork for the city’s current success.
As a Shanghai-born patriot born into a shipping family, Tung had a strong network of influential global contacts. He put them to use in service of the nation in his lifelong efforts to advance dialogue between China and the US. He is one of the few Hong Kong politicians to have officially met two US presidents, Bill Clinton and George W Bush.
This weekend, a state funeral will be held to honour Tung, who was also a former vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). There will be a vigil on Saturday and a memorial on Sunday, while condolence books will be opened for the public at multiple venues from Friday to Sunday.
Tung is the third Hongkonger to be accorded a state funeral, following industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Shi Taifeng, a Politburo member and top vice-chairman of the CPPCC, is overseeing the arrangements.
The South China Morning Post is running a special commemorative print supplement on Saturday, sharing reflections from those who knew Tung personally.
Join us for part one, which features tributes from past and present officials and other political figures. You can also find other tributes from the supplement here and here.

Goh Chok Tong, emeritus senior minister and former prime minister of Singapore
My friendship with Tung Chee-hwa goes back to the early 1970s, when we were both in the shipping industry. Together with three other shipping lines, we formed a container consortium in the Far East-Europe route.
Our friendship developed and endured as we went on to lead Singapore and Hong Kong, respectively. CH first visited Singapore as chief executive in 1997, and I made my return visit as prime minister in 2000.
In our numerous meetings, we discussed the challenges that Singapore and Hong Kong faced and explored opportunities to strengthen bilateral relations. Later, he was preoccupied with getting the United States and China to understand each other better. He was well-placed as he had influential friends in both countries.
I have always enjoyed meeting CH. He was a helpful, sincere and trustworthy friend who exuded humility and warmth. I will miss him dearly.

Leung Chun-ying, vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference
A solemn tribute to Mr Tung Chee-hwa, the first chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, vice-chairman of the 10th to 13th National Committees of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), and vice-chairman of the Preparatory Committee for the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the National People’s Congress.
Mr Tung spearheaded the establishment of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and its government. Earning the highest trust of the nation, he implemented the principles of “one country, two systems”, “Hong Kong people administering Hong Kong”, and a high degree of autonomy, while charting the course for Hong Kong’s long-term development and addressing the city’s deep-rooted livelihood issues.
Kind-hearted, wise, and principled, Mr Tung was a true exemplar of leadership and service.
May Mr Tung rest in peace.
(from Leung’s Facebook post)

Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor, former chief executive of Hong Kong
I deeply mourn the passing of Mr Tung Chee-hwa and extend my profound condolences to Mrs Tung and their family.
As the first chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Mr Tung guided Hong Kong into a new era under “one country, two systems” with profound patriotism, extensive international experience, and a humble approach to governance – a monumental legacy that serves our present and benefits generations to come.
With insight into Hong Kong’s deep-seated social challenges, he mapped out long-term strategic plans for housing, education and elderly care.
Having served as director of social welfare during his tenure, I profoundly felt his care for the elderly. As a younger fellow native of Zhoushan in Zhejiang, I will always remember Mr Tung as a truly benevolent elder. How fondly I cherish the memories of having lighthearted conversations with him at his home.
I pay my highest respects and deepest tribute to Mr Tung Chee-hwa.

Donald Tsang Yam-kuen, former chief executive of Hong Kong
I first met CH in the 1990s, when we served together on the then Executive Council. From the outset, I was struck by his gentle grace and breadth of vision. He guided Hong Kong masterfully through the historic transition in 1997, setting out, with extraordinary foresight, his priorities for the administration of Hong Kong by the people of Hong Kong.
Working under his leadership, I witnessed first-hand his selfless and tireless devotion. He worked long hours every day, through weekends and throughout the year; holidays scarcely featured during his term of office.
Through his unwavering dedication, he transformed tertiary education, raising enrolment from 14 to 50 per cent. Drawing on his extensive experience and commercial networks, he opened vital diplomatic doors with the United States, creating valuable new opportunities for Hong Kong’s trade and strengthening bilateral relations.
CH also successfully championed the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement, securing a vital economic foundation for Hong Kong’s development and closer integration with mainland China. When Hong Kong was battered by the Asian financial crisis, he gave me his unreserved support as we fought off unscrupulous speculators. And when the Sars epidemic struck, his quiet resolve helped steer us through the storm.
I shall forever cherish CH’s gentle smile, gracious disposition, unyielding spirit and profound patriotism. He devoted his life to Hong Kong, and his legacy will endure.

Andrew Li Kwok-nang, chief justice of Hong Kong from 1997 to 2010
I have known Mr Tung well for over 35 years.
As chief executive, he respected the rule of law with an independent judiciary.
He is one of the finest men I have the privilege of knowing. He was patriotic and served the motherland and Hong Kong with selfless dedication. He was a visionary leader who influenced the course of history. He had utmost integrity, courage, perseverance and wisdom.
He always set a good example and had a great generosity of spirit.
He was a gentleman in the Confucian tradition. I have never heard him bad-mouth any person. He always addressed the matter and not the individual person.
Over the years, I learned a great deal from him. In particular, I learned the importance of humility and that, as a leader, one must have broad shoulders and put people in the right places.

Henry Tang Ying-yen, former financial secretary of Hong Kong
Mr Tung was a visionary leader with a warm heart. He was always kind, patient and thoughtful towards those around him. I was honoured to work with him, to benefit from his wisdom, and to be inspired by his persistence, impartiality and benevolence.
Amid political pressure and economic challenges, he remained committed to protecting and preserving Hong Kong’s interests under “one country, two systems”.
To me, Mr Tung demonstrated not only the qualities of great leadership, but also the values that truly elevate Hong Kong.
He inspired and encouraged me to shoulder greater responsibilities as financial secretary during critical times, and I will never forget that.
His devotion to Hong Kong and the motherland set an excellent example for all of us to follow.
Mr Tung may be gone from this world, but he will never be gone from my heart. I believe the same is true for the people of Hong Kong.

Bernard Charnwut Chan, former convenor of the Executive Council of Hong Kong
Though my late parents were long-time friends of Mr Tung Chee-hwa and his wife Betty, my personal journey with him began when I joined the Legislative Council in 1998. Appointing me to the Executive Council in 2004 and later inviting me to Our Hong Kong Foundation in 2017, he gave me the privilege of observing his tireless dedication first-hand.
Behind the scenes, Mr Tung worked round-the-clock with extraordinary magnanimity. He never harboured anger towards critics, striving instead to bring diverse stakeholders together to address deep-seated challenges in our economy, housing, and youth development. It was his evident authenticity and profound, genuine love for both our country and city that inspired so many of us to rally behind him and contribute. Even when he could have chosen a quiet retirement with his family, he continued to serve selflessly.
Above all, Mr Tung was a kind man with a generous heart. I will forever cherish his warmth, wisdom and steadfast friendship.

Regina Ip Lau Suk-yee, convenor of the Executive Council of Hong Kong
I worked for Mr Tung for seven years as director of immigration and then as secretary for security. He was a visionary leader – the first to promote Hong Kong as a global tech hub.
He had extensive global connections and Hong Kong benefited immensely from his international connectivity. He was highly respected by many global leaders.
As a person, he was a caring and considerate boss. When I was studying at Stanford University, he visited me in my apartment and invited me to dinner in San Francisco from time to time.

Frederick Ma Si-hang, chairman of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council
Meeting Mr Tung Chee-hwa changed my life. His invitation to enter public service gave me a new purpose and a lasting sense of responsibility to Hong Kong.
I deeply respect his dedication to Hong Kong and his vision for realising “one country, two systems”. His efforts to develop technology and innovation, his foresight in opening up the mainland market for Hong Kong, and his work to improve people’s lives are a powerful reminder of what public service means.
What I cherish most is the man behind the public role. His integrity and sincerity have left an indelible impression on me, and his trust inspired me to persevere through difficulties and serve with dedication.
To me, Mr Tung will always be more than the leader who brought me into government. He is someone whose example continues to guide and inspire me every day.

data.title: ‘In hard times, your honour shines’: Jack Ma pays tribute to Tung Chee-hwa
data.description:
Alibaba Group co-founder Jack Ma reflects on his ties to Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa. Those connections spanned both business and philanthropy, encompassing Tung’s eight years on Alibaba’s board of directors and his inspirational role in Ma’s youth entrepreneurship foundation for local youths.
Ma’s reflections are part of the South China Morning Post’s special commemorative print supplement published on Saturday.
I knew Mr Tung for many years. When he served as the chief executive of Hong Kong, Alibaba was expanding its businesses in the city. As we pursued our mission to “make it easy to do business anywhere”, Mr Tung offered us invaluable guidance and care.
After he stepped down as chief executive, I invited him to serve as one of the inaugural independent directors on Alibaba’s board in 2014, a role he graciously accepted. We were privileged to work alongside him for eight years.

During his tenure as an independent director, Mr Tung was exceptionally conscientious and dedicated. With profound wisdom and vision, he staunchly supported Alibaba’s innovations across various fields. He appreciated the core values of integrity and kindness that define Alibaba and he looked forward to seeing the company expand globally and earn the world’s respect as a Chinese enterprise.
Although Mr Tung has passed away, Alibaba’s continued development serves to realise his aspirations. I believe this is the finest tribute we can pay to his memory.

The qualities Mr Tung demonstrated during our years together had a profound impact on both me and Alibaba. He possessed a deep devotion to the country, matched with a forward-looking, global perspective. He was a tireless innovator who remained pragmatic and humble. He viewed the encouragement and mentorship of young people as his lifelong, unwavering duty.
Over a decade ago, inspired by his vision and call to action, we launched the Alibaba Hong Kong Young Entrepreneurs Foundation to help young people realise their dreams of innovation and entrepreneurship. This foundation stands as part of Mr Tung’s enduring legacy.
Gone is the man, enduring is his legacy.
Standing steady for the nation and city; in hard times, your honour shines.
Sharing great responsibilities shoulder to shoulder, as a mentor and friend, your unwavering devotion will be remembered.

data.title: Foreign carer scheme may drive up wages, leave poor without help, employers warn
data.description:
A new pilot scheme to bring in foreign domestic carers for the elderly to deal with an ageing population could disrupt Hong Kong’s existing helper market, driving up wages and putting care beyond the reach of low-income older residents, some employers and agencies have warned.
They said the measure, announced by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in his policy address on Wednesday, was likely to prompt existing helpers to demand higher pay or quit to take up the new employment opportunity, adding to families’ financial burden.
Authorities revealed on Friday that the minimum wage for carers under the pilot scheme would be 10 to 20 per cent higher than that for existing helpers. The current minimum allowable wage for helpers is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month.
Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Domestic Helpers Association, said 30 per cent of the city’s more than 378,000 foreign domestic helpers were already caring for elderly people, questioning the need for a separate category of workers.
“There are many low-income people in Hong Kong who are retired but need a domestic worker to take care of them,” she said.
“But with expected rising wages for workers, how can the government help these families? The new measure could lead to only the well-off being able to afford it.”


Yung added that some employers feared helpers would move to the new scheme to earn more, leaving families struggling to recruit workers to care for children and other family members in need.
She also questioned whether authorities could monitor whether carers had completed the required training and met the qualification requirements before arriving in Hong Kong under the scheme.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that the newly created jobs were unlikely to have an impact on the helpers’ market. He said existing helpers hoping to switch to the new role would have to return to their home country to receive relevant training and meet other requirements before they could return to Hong Kong to take up the carer job.
Lee announced that the government would admit carers with more advanced training and experience in elderly care on a pilot basis, under a scheme modelled on the city’s existing foreign domestic helper regime, to help meet the home-care needs of older residents.
A government source said those employed under the new scheme, to be launched next year, must have experience in caring for the elderly and undergo relevant training in their home countries.
Thomas Chan Tung-fung, chairman of the Hong Kong Union of Employment Agencies, said it was expected that carers admitted under the new scheme would be paid more.
“If you require a worker, in addition to doing housework, to also have special skills such as medical care skills, the worker will require a higher salary,” he said.




Chan said helpers equipped with such skills currently earned about HK$1,500 to HK$2,500 a month above the minimum allowable wage.
“Currently, 30 per cent of helpers are caring for elderly residents or patients, most of them earning a monthly salary of HK$5,100. If the new carer scheme is implemented in the future, it might lead workers doing the same type of job to question why there is unequal pay for equal work,” he said.
This could prompt some helpers to demand a pay rise or quit to join the new scheme, he said.
“It could inadvertently drive up costs for employers,” he said.
While acknowledging the demand for elderly care in ageing Hong Kong, Chan urged authorities to provide allowances for families under financial pressure to hire carers under the scheme.

Phobsuk Gasing, chairwoman of the Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions, also questioned the necessity of the new scheme, calling instead for recognition of current helpers’ work through better wages.
“Domestic workers have already been doing this job. Our skills should be recognised with better pay,” she said.
The pilot scheme was among a series of measures Lee announced in the policy address to build an age-friendly society.
In Hong Kong, the number of people aged 65 and above is projected to nearly double from 1.45 million in 2021 to 2.74 million by 2046, when more than one in three residents will be elderly.
Despite concerns from employers and helpers, experts and NGOs said the new scheme to bring in skilled domestic carers could help meet some families’ elderly care needs but called for more to be done.
Chou Kee-lee, chair professor of social policy at the Education University of Hong Kong, said the scheme would make it easier for households to find workers specifically trained to care for older family members.
“The scheme will enable a systematic approach with clearer standards for assessing whether carers are qualified to perform more complex care procedures,” he said.
Chou suggested that authorities model the qualifications for foreign carers on the requirements for workers caring for elderly residents in the city’s care homes, which he said would increase public confidence in them.
But he added that the measure would mainly benefit better-off households, as low-income families might not be able to afford carers under the scheme, calling for more support for these families.
The Society for Community Organisation described the pilot scheme as an innovative approach to meeting the home-care needs of older residents but suggested that the government subsidise people to hire carers.
It also urged the government to ensure the workers possessed basic local language communication skills and training in medical or caregiving work to meet older residents’ needs.

data.title: A man who built bridges over walls: SCMP’s Tammy Tam on Tung Chee-hwa
data.description:
South China Morning Post publisher Tammy Tam reflects on her encounters with Hong Kong’s first chief executive, the late Tung Chee-hwa, looking back on memories from her days as a frontline reporter, his regular exchanges with media representatives and Tung’s rare appearance at an SCMP conference in 2020 to advocate US-China dialogue.
Her recollections are part of a special SCMP commemorative supplement that features heavyweights from various sectors paying tribute to Tung.
“Are you Ms Tam? Mr Tung wants to speak to you.”
The call from former chief executive Tung Chee-hwa’s office came shortly after I joined the South China Morning Post more than a decade ago.
It was at a time when Hong Kong’s newspaper of record was busy preparing its annual flagship China Conference event. Tung was always among those at the top of the guest list for the event since its inaugural edition in 2015.
Now that he is gone, the memories come flooding back.
As a journalist, I started to encounter Tung from 1996, when the Sino-British talks over Hong Kong’s future entered their final stage, and the then shipping tycoon emerged as the most likely candidate to lead Hong Kong after the transfer of sovereignty in 1997.
We reporters door-stepped, hounded and grilled him regularly, both before he became chief executive and throughout his seven years in the post. We would not let him go even after he stepped down to become a state leader as a vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body.

Tung was well known for his humble and unpretentious personality, although he was understandably a bit camera-shy in the beginning and did not necessarily like answering the questions we yelled out at him. He would run the media gauntlet by simply waving with a “hello, good morning” as he walked past us, but always with a smile on his face.
Of course, he would meet senior members of the media regularly during and after his tenure as chief executive to exchange views on many pressing issues pertaining to the city and the wider world. I remember how he would always pick the same classic Shanghai restaurant, which led to some of us developing a real taste for Shanghainese cuisine.
That morning more than 10 years ago, when his office put me on the line with him, Tung’s voice was as warm and familiar as in my frontline reporting days.
“Tammy, I’m very glad that you are now with the SCMP, so I’m calling just to share with you some more background information on why the China-US relationship matters,” he said.
“I do hope the SCMP can explain the latest about China to your global audience, and break down the most important bilateral relationship in language that people can understand – I don’t mean just writing something in English, but using words that matter and make sense for everyone to grasp your meaning.”

I have never forgotten that piece of advice and encouragement from Tung. The South China Morning Post positions itself as a highly credible go-to source for comprehensive and meaningful Greater China news, starting with what happens in our home city by sticking to fair and fact-based journalism.
We unbox the complexities and bring out the nuances in our China and Hong Kong coverage, reading between the lines to glean the information that matters, and present it using the kind of language needed for better understanding. Not just in English, as Tung said.
The last time I saw him was in December 2020, when he graciously accepted our invitation to speak again at the China Conference. We were in the middle of the Covid crisis and it was risky for elderly people in particular to be out and about socialising, but Tung put on a mask to attend our event, along with his beloved wife, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping.
While this was a virtual conference attended online by hundreds from around the world, Tung made a physical appearance in our studio to read out his keynote speech on camera, which was then broadcast live. He went off script and kept emphasising how “we can solve all the problems” if only Beijing and Washington would work together.
Looking back, I realised Tung was well aware that his health problems might soon keep him away from public activities and he felt the need to seize every opportunity to speak up while he still could. I learned later that he was already under his doctor’s advice to reduce public engagements as much as possible. But it was typical of him to keep his word and set aside inconveniences if he felt what he was doing was meaningful for everyone else.
There was another phone call from his office that is still etched in my memory – this time on a summer’s day in July 2008.
“Ms Tam, this is from Mr Tung’s office. He wants to invite you to the August 8 Beijing Olympics opening!”
It had been quite a while since I had last talked to him, and I was gobsmacked by what seemed to be an invitation from out of the blue. Then I remembered what it was all about.
Back in 2001, when I was a television journalist, my crew and I followed Tung all the way to and across the United States for his meeting with then president Bill Clinton. It was a roadshow for Hong Kong’s “one country, two systems” governing formula, but Tung was also pushing for China’s accession to the World Trade Organization, and was on a “secret” mission to convince Washington not to openly oppose China’s bid for the Olympics.

Come July 13, 2001, Tung was anxiously waiting for the announcement on television in his US hotel suite, where we had gathered for a live interview.
“The Games of the 29th Olympiad in 2008 are awarded to the city of Beijing,” International Olympic Committee president Juan Antonio Samaranch announced, delighting all of us glued to the screen. An excited and jubilant Tung made an announcement of his own right there and then: “I’ll invite all of you in this room to Beijing in 2008!”
And there I was, seven years later, realising that Tung had really meant what he said and remembered to save a ticket for me. I told his office that I had already secured my media credentials to cover the Games and suggested the precious ticket should go to someone more in need.
My phone rang again 10 minutes later and I was told: “Mr Tung agrees with your suggestion, but he insists on inviting you to a celebration dinner hosted by him when he arrives in Beijing ahead of the opening.” I accepted without hesitation.
Over the years, my colleagues and I at the SCMP have received groups of visiting American students and academics touring Hong Kong and the mainland, sponsored by the China-US Exchange Foundation set up by Tung using his own money.
These visits present opportunities for candid and engaging conversations on many sensitive and thorny issues – just the kind of thing we need to enhance mutual understanding on both sides of the geopolitical divide.
Tung was 89 years old when he left us, but it still feels too soon, considering how much more there is to do in the mission he dedicated the last decades of his life to.
I have never found the right moment to say this to him until now: thank you, Mr Tung, for your leadership, generosity, kindness, sincerity and genuine love for our city and nation; we will never forget you, and we will always remember the shining example you have set in building bridges over walls for everyone’s benefit.

data.title: Hong Kong civil servants to get hourly leave but businesses unlikely to follow
data.description:
Hong Kong civil servants could receive flexible hourly family care leave next year as part of the government’s wider drive to boost birth rates, the South China Morning Post has learned, though business leaders warn the private sector has little incentive to follow suit, citing manpower and financial constraints, especially for smaller firms.
Under the “promote fertility” section of Wednesday’s policy address, the government said it would introduce family care leave for its employees to enhance family-friendly measures.
A government source said that civil servants could apply for leave by the hour for personal matters, such as accompanying family members to hospital or attending parent-teacher meetings.
The Civil Service Bureau was formulating details and would conduct further consultation with government employees, the insider added.
Tsoi Koon-lung, president of the Hong Kong Chinese Civil Servants’ Association, welcomed the proposal, saying it would give colleagues greater flexibility.
He said he expected each civil servant to receive an annual entitlement of 10 to 12 hours, with the arrangement taking effect in early 2027.
Currently, even staff who needed only one or two hours for family matters had to take at least half a day off, Tsoi said.
“Some civil servants feel this wastes their annual leave, while the government ends up short-staffed for half a day,” he said.
The hourly system would allow civil servants to respond to family matters more flexibly without wasting their annual leave, he added.
But Tsoi also cautioned that the entitlement might be insufficient for those with multiple children and called for ongoing reviews.
“After the implementation, the government should constantly monitor the use of such leave to see if many colleagues report that the entitlement is insufficient.”
Ngan Man-him, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Federation of Civil Service Unions, echoed Tsoi’s view, adding that the application procedures should also be simple and flexible so that civil servants could better respond to different emergencies.
“For emergencies, we might just tell our boss the reason via WhatsApp and then complete the procedure with supporting documents afterwards. We hope to keep it simple,” he said.

Labour sector lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, also an honorary adviser to the Hong Kong Civil Servants General Union, said the measure could encourage young government workers to start a family.
“Some youngsters can enjoy a relatively stable working environment after joining the civil service, and they would be more inclined to have children with such family-friendly measures,” he said.
Lam added that the government could act as a role model for the private sector, although adoption could be difficult, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
“For SMEs, their resources and manpower are short, and they may find it difficult to make such arrangements,” he said.
Lam added that such arrangements would also put greater financial pressure on private-sector employers, making them reluctant to follow the government’s lead.
“The government can do the maths, and if the budget permits, it could consider paying the wages on such days off on behalf of the private sector so that all workers in Hong Kong can benefit from family leave.”
Danny Lau Tat-pong, ­honorary life chairman of the Hong Kong Small and Medium Enterprises Association, said even if the government were to subsidise family leave wages, it would still be difficult for SMEs to make such arrangements.
“Even if the government pays the salaries, we are still short-staffed,” he said. “When employees are only away for a few hours, it is impossible for us to hire a part-timer to fill in.”
Lau added that while private firms might avoid formal family leave policies, employers typically granted short, discretionary leave for emergencies.
Lawmaker Jonathan Lamport, who also represents the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, said larger corporations with more resources would be more likely to adopt the practice.
“In a micro-enterprise with only a few staff, ad hoc leave can significantly disrupt daily operations because there is simply no buffer,” he said.
“We hope the government can act as a partner by providing practical incentives – such as tax concessions to help SMEs overcome these operational hurdles and build a family-friendly workplace.”
The government is the largest employer in Hong Kong, with more than 170,000 civil servants.
In 2024, it introduced childcare leave for staff, entitling each civil servant to three days of leave annually for each child under three years old.

data.title: Patient who needed soft food dies after choking on regular meal at public hospital
data.description:
A Hong Kong patient died after suffering a heart attack when he was fed a regular meal instead of the required soft food and choked at Prince of Wales Hospital.
The public hospital in Sha Tin issued a public apology on Friday and said it had appointed an eight-person panel to look into the blunder.
A report, along with recommendations for improvement measures, is expected in eight weeks.
The 54-year-old male patient was admitted to hospital on Wednesday morning “due to deteriorated mental status”, the Hospital Authority said in a statement reporting the sentinel event.
The man had no identification document upon admission, so the hospital generated a “pseudo identifier” for registration.
Given his clinical condition, the attending doctor subsequently gave a “diet as tolerated”, or DAT, order for nursing staff.
DAT generally refers to a medical instruction indicating that a patient should consume food and fluids according to his or her individual tolerance and comfort level.
But the hospital’s catering management system defaults to arranging a regular meal for patients registered under a pseudo identifier.
“A nursing staff member did not complete checking the patient’s previous diet records to adjust the diet order, [and] a regular meal was served to the patient that night,” the hospital said.
He started feeling unwell while fed by a patient care assistant.
Doctors were called to help remove the obstruction in the patient’s airway, but during the emergency treatment, he went into cardiac arrest.
His condition continued to deteriorate, and he died late that night.
“Upon reviewing the patient’s history after the incident, the hospital found that the patient had been frequently hospitalised before due to underlying diseases,” the authority said.
The patient was said to have suffered from dementia and had a history of stroke.
“Following speech therapy assessment, a purée diet was recommended for the patient due to dysphagia,” it said, referring to difficulty swallowing.
The hospital said it was deeply saddened by the death and had met with the patient’s family to explain the incident, extending its sincere apologies and condolences.
“The hospital has devised immediate measures, including reminding healthcare staff to thoroughly assess patients’ clinical conditions and diet orders before making meal arrangements and reviewing the default meal setting of the [dietary and catering management] system,” it said.
“The nursing staff member and [patient care assistant] concerned have been temporarily arranged for non-clinical duties.”
A similar blunder was reported at Caritas Medical Centre in March last year when a 75-year-old patient choked to death after a nurse misunderstood the doctor’s instructions due to a communication error and gave him the wrong food.
The man, who was supposed to be on a puréed diet, was fed solid food instead.

data.title: Tesla auditing Chinese suppliers ahead of Optimus roll-out: sources
data.description:
Tesla officials and engineers have begun auditing part of the firm’s Chinese supply chain, as Elon Musk’s company aims to quickly ramp up production of its Optimus humanoid robot after it hits the global market later this year, according to sources with knowledge of the matter.
Chinese companies set to undergo supplier audits included heat-control component manufacturer Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, auto parts supplier Ningbo Joyson Electronic, and chassis producer Tuopu Group, two corporate executives with business ties to the manufacturers told the South China Morning Post.
Most of the firms being examined by Tesla as potential Optimus suppliers already provide automotive components used in the company’s electric cars, and they are all based in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.
A supplier audit is a process in which a vendor’s production and compliance standards are evaluated to ensure product quality.
According to the sources, this round of audits comes as Tesla plans to place additional orders for components, as mass production of the firm’s Optimus robots will soon begin at its plant in Fremont, California.
Tesla China declined to comment on the issue.
Tesla is locked in a race with several competitors in the United States and China to mass produce humanoid robots – artificial intelligence-powered robots that can be deployed in scenarios ranging from factory production lines to elderly care centres.


In January, Tesla signalled it was pivoting towards becoming a physical AI firm, with CEO Elon Musk announcing the company would halt production of its Model S and Model X cars in Fremont so the plant could focus on building robots.
The Chinese vendors had signed non-disclosure agreements with Tesla, which would subject them to penalties worth millions of dollars if they failed to comply, the sources said.
“The audits show that those Chinese suppliers are an important part of Optimus’ supply chain,” said Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service consultancy. “They enjoy cost and technological advantages over their domestic and overseas rivals.”
Chinese carmakers such as Xpeng were viewed as strong rivals to Tesla in robotics due to their manufacturing heft and complete, cost-effective supply chains, analysts said.
In December, Musk endorsed Xpeng’s Iron humanoid robot on social media while predicting Chinese companies would ­dominate the global robotics market alongside Tesla.
In April, Tesla’s China president, Allan Wang Hao, said the company’s Shanghai Gigafactory had the potential to produce humanoid robots, as it benefited from China’s complete supply chain and advanced manufacturing techniques.

data.title: Alibaba open-sources AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts.
The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was designed to analyse contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and identify a broad range of diseases and other abnormalities, such as malignant tumours, the institute said on Friday.
The model was trained using CT scans paired with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, it achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect diagnostic accuracy.
The research team said the training method could eventually be extended to other types of medical imaging, calling the model “the world’s first expert-level generalist medical imaging model”.
In a comparative study involving 26 human radiologists from multiple hospitals, the model’s average accuracy exceeded that of 23 participants, according to the study. With the model’s help, the radiologists also managed to improve their ability to prevent missed diagnoses by 10 per cent while reducing the time required by more than 30 per cent, Damo said.
The research was published on Thursday in the journal Science. Several institutions took part in the study alongside Alibaba, including a hospital affiliated with Zhejiang University.
The model’s release builds on a string of recent medical AI advances by Alibaba as Chinese technology giants increasingly explore the use of cutting-edge technology in healthcare settings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
In recent years, Damo Academy has focused on developing AI screening tools to help doctors identify conditions including pancreatic, stomach and colorectal cancers, as well as aortic dissections.
In April, the division released the Coca AI model, which it said was more sensitive than radiologists in spotting early-stage colorectal cancer from CT scans. The model was co-developed with Chinese institutions including the Guangdong General Hospital.

data.title: Foreign carers for elderly to get 10 to 20% more pay than current helpers
data.description:
Foreign domestic carers brought to Hong Kong to look after elderly residents under a proposed government pilot scheme would receive 10 to 20 per cent more pay than existing helpers, the labour minister has said.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han on Friday revealed additional details about the arrangement for foreign domestic carers, as the government also released a comprehensive report outlining strategies for an ageing society.
The report listed 73 measures spanning 11 areas, many of which were revealed in the policy address earlier this week.
“The rapid development of the ageing population has an immense impact on the economy and different areas of society, and both challenges and opportunities exist,” Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk Wing-hing said.
“The government must actively formulate strategies as early as possible based on population changes and make forward-looking plans.”
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced in last year’s policy address the formation of a working group on ageing society strategies, chaired by Cheuk and tasked with submitting a report on the blueprint this year.
The pilot scheme to introduce foreign domestic carers, announced in the policy address on Wednesday, is among measures to tackle manpower shortages exacerbated by the greying population.
Sun said the minimum wage for carers would be 10 to 20 per cent higher than that of current domestic helpers. The carers must also receive elderly care training recognised by Hong Kong and possess at least three years of experience looking after older people.

The current minimum wage for helpers is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month.
“People can choose,” Sun said. “If you only need a foreign helper, you can continue to recruit from the foreign helpers’ market.
“But if you need someone with greater ability and they are accredited to take care of elderly people, you can pay a bit more to hire a foreign domestic carer.”
The minister added that the initiative would provide reassurance to local families seeking workers with proven experience in caring for elderly people.
Hong Kong is struggling with a rapidly ageing population. The number of people aged 65 and older is projected to increase from about 1.8 million in 2025 to 2.74 million by 2046, at which point more than one in three residents will be elderly.
Sun expressed confidence that the scheme would not disrupt the market for foreign helpers.
“If existing helpers want to change their job and become foreign domestic carers, they would need to return to their home country, receive relevant training and meet other requirements before they can come to Hong Kong,” he said.
“We do not want the newly created job causing concern to current [employers] of foreign domestic helpers.”
A government source on Wednesday said that the scheme would be launched next year.
Alice Lau Yim, permanent secretary for labour and welfare, said the carers would be required to work in a domestic setting and live with their employers, similar to the current arrangement for helpers.
“The main target is to raise the quality of foreign domestic helpers who are now taking care of elderly people and offer one more option in the market to families in need,” she said.
Currently, about 380,000 foreign domestic helpers work in Hong Kong. More than half are from the Philippines, followed by Indonesia and other countries.
But Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Overseas Domestic Helpers Association, warned that the scheme could disrupt the market for domestic helpers.
She said the government had consulted employers’ groups beforehand but decided to press ahead despite opposition.
Yung noted many helpers had already undergone training before coming to Hong Kong and had been caring for elderly people for several years, making specialised carers unnecessary.
“Some dissatisfied helpers may just leave their jobs for better pay and higher status … and their flight back home [for the training] is covered by the employers,” she said.
She also highlighted the financial burden on employers, claiming that they already spent about HK$7,000 a month to cover the wages and living-in costs of helpers.

data.title: Ant International launches AI overhaul to automate global financial operations
data.description:
Ant International, the overseas affiliate of China’s Ant Group, is executing an artificial intelligence overhaul across its entire suite of global financial services, introducing AI agents designed to help manage payments, foreign exchange and treasury operations.
Described by the company as its largest-ever product upgrade, the initiative embeds AI-native solutions across all platforms: cross-border payment network Alipay+, merchant services provider Antom, account and treasury platform WorldFirst, and digital credit platform Bettr.
The global roll-out has begun and would extend through winter, the company said.
Peng Yang, CEO of Ant International, said the shift would prepare global commerce for a “fully agentised future”, adding that fintech providers needed “a future-ready trust infrastructure” paired with financial AI models and connected AI-native solutions.
The move follows a roughly US$1.2 billion series A funding round in July, backed by Ant Group, Alibaba Group Holding and other institutional investors.
Carved out as an independent operating entity in 2024, Ant International said it connects over 150 million merchants to more than 2 billion consumer accounts, processing over 25 million daily transactions across 210 markets.
The upgrade spans nearly 100 products, including AI assistants for payments and account management, tools for cash-flow forecasting, currency hedging and global payouts, and services supporting billing, tax filing, marketing and access to credit. Ant said it also introduced a business account designed for AI agents.
“We’re a problem solver for merchants,” Gary Liu, CEO of Antom, said in an interview with the South China Morning Post, noting that 89.5 per cent of Antom’s merchants already used AI agents, with 81.4 per cent of payment tasks receiving AI assistance.

Liu said agent authorisation should depend on the task and its spending limits, rather than the job titles used to determine employees’ authority. “It matters what the task is,” he said.
According to Ant International, the overhaul relies on two proprietary systems: a payment foundation model - called Antom 3-in-1 Transformer - that processes structured records, sequences of behaviour and relationships between users, merchants and devices to assess transactions, and FalconTST, a forecasting model for cash flows and currency exposures.
Ant International said FalconTST had achieved over 93 per cent forecasting accuracy and reduced corporate currency hedging and capital allocation costs by 30 to 60 per cent in real-world applications.
On top of the Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, the company built a second security layer, with a “know-your-agent” (KYA) framework linked to its Agentic Mobile Protocol, which connects mobile wallet networks to agentic transactions. The security layer includes AgentSafePay, which offers a fund-back guarantee against losses from agent-specific risks.
To combat security risks tied to autonomous transactions, the firm relies on its Antom Shield framework to guard against AI-driven fraud, as well as AgentSafePay, an indemnity scheme covering merchant losses from agent errors.
Ant International is also partnering with Visa and Mastercard to establish global agent verification standards through its Agentic Mobile Protocol.
Alibaba is the owner of SCMP.

data.title: CUHK department triggers backlash over WeChat attendance registration policy
data.description:
A department at Hong Kong’s second-oldest university has faced backlash over asking students to use mainland Chinese messaging app WeChat to register their attendance and keep its location services enabled, before later saying the arrangement was optional.
The policy was revealed after a screenshot of an email from the information engineering department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) was posted to the social media platform Threads on Friday.
“Starting from the next class, attendance will be recorded by scanning a QR code through WeChat. Please install the WeChat app and enable location services before coming to class,” the email said.
“Your attendance will be considered valid only if your location is detected within the classroom, such as CUHK faculty of law, CUHK Library Road, CUHK Lee Shau Kee Building.”
It added that a test QR code had been provided to students to ensure the app was working properly.
The post attracted hundreds of replies and was forwarded thousands of times.
Some students questioned online why the department had not adopted the university’s own app for checking student attendance.
The South China Morning Post has approached CUHK and the department for comment.

Other users also criticised the department and staff for using an app other than CUHK’s to track attendance and raised concerns about potential data leaks.
“Am I studying in mainland China now or what?” the author of the post, nemui._.desuyo, wrote.
The user wrote that he had already sent an email to the department to follow up on the matter and ask why it had not adopted the CUHK-developed app instead.
“How can they force us to install a third-party app just for taking attendance? Who’s going to be responsible if there’s a security breach?” another commenter said.
A user named iireneliui wrote: “CUHK has its own attendance system, plus card readers to tap student IDs. Or worst-case scenario, just use a plain old sign-in sheet. Why on earth do we have to use WeChat?”
The department later sent an email to students clarifying that they could use either WeChat or sign a paper attendance sheet in class.
“You only need to use one of these two methods. If you do not normally use WeChat, there is no need to install it just to record your attendance,” the email stated.
However, the email said students would still need to enable location services if they chose to use WeChat.
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data said it had not received any inquiries or complaints about the matter, adding that it would not comment on individual cases.
The privacy watchdog also said personal data should only be collected for lawful purposes directly related to a function or activity by the relevant organisation, provided the information was “necessary, adequate but not excessive”.

data.title: China’s top AI models generate just 10% of OpenAI, Anthropic revenue: report
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence models from seven major developers combined generate only about 10 per cent of the revenue reported for OpenAI and Anthropic, even as investor enthusiasm remains intense, according to US-based research firm Rhodium Group.
The Chinese AI models earned an estimated US$10.7 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) from March to August, a fraction of the more than US$100 billion combined for OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Rhodium report published on Thursday.
The report covers DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, MiniMax, Alibaba Group Holding, ByteDance and Kuaishou Technology, which runs the Kling AI video generator.
ARR, a widely used measure for fast-growing companies, projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period.
ByteDance led the Chinese group in ARR at US$4 billion as of July, followed by Alibaba at US$2.4 billion in August. By comparison, OpenAI reached US$40 billion in August and Anthropic was at US$65 billion in July.

DeepSeek and Kling had the lowest ARR among the major Chinese AI companies tracked by Rhodium, at US$500 million each as of June and March, respectively. They were followed by MiniMax at US$800 million and Moonshot at US$1 billion, both as of August.
Executives at Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, told investors on Wednesday that the company’s ARR had reached US$1.8 billion. The report stated that Z.ai’s ARR from its API business was US$1.6 billion in August.
Despite the gap, investors have continued to pile into Chinese AI companies. Rhodium said their valuations remained “substantially lower” than those of OpenAI and Anthropic, and some looked far more expensive relative to revenue.
Moonshot has been undergoing a funding round that could value it at roughly US$50 billion and has filed confidentially for a Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO), while DeepSeek was also nearing the completion of a pre-IPO funding round valuing it at about 500 billion yuan (US$74 billion), the South China Morning Post reported previously.
Meanwhile, Anthropic was expected to go public later this year with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, according to media reports. OpenAI had discussed a new funding round that would value it at about US$1.2 trillion, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
“Valuations relative to revenue appear exorbitant for Moonshot and DeepSeek at present,” the Rhodium report said. Their estimated valuation-to-ARR multiples stood at 50 times and 163 times, respectively, compared with 34 times for OpenAI and 21 times for Anthropic.
The numbers underscore a central challenge for China’s AI industry: how to turn AI models into sustainable businesses while spending heavily to keep pace at the technological frontier.
Revenues for these Chinese AI companies have grown rapidly. Z.ai recorded a 400 per cent increase year on year in first-half revenue to 953.9 million yuan, while MiniMax’s revenue surged 283 per cent to US$116.6 million during the same period.
Still, Z.ai and MiniMax, both listed in Hong Kong, could remain loss-making through 2030 due to spending required for computing power, Macquarie Group’s head of Asia internet and software research Ellie Jiang told the SCMP last week. Investors have so far been willing to tolerate those losses while AI adoption remains at an early stage, she said.

The findings come as Chinese developers have rapidly narrowed the performance gap with their US counterparts while competing aggressively on price and embracing open-source and open-weight models.
However, the open-weight strategy has made Chinese models harder to monetise, Rhodium said. Third-party cloud providers can deploy open-weight models and sell access without paying the original developer.
“This could be changing, as Moonshot and Alibaba are pushing for revenue-sharing agreements with major users of their open-weight models,” Rhodium said. For example, Moonshot was in discussions with Microsoft, Amazon and Google, with its potential share of revenue reaching as much as 30 per cent, Reuters reported last month.
Alibaba owns the SCMP.

data.title: Asia-Pacific firms divided on how AI will impact office space demand: survey
data.description:
Nearly one-fifth of surveyed companies in the Asia-Pacific region believe wider adoption of artificial intelligence will reduce their real estate needs, a new study by CBRE has found.
More than half – 56 per cent – held a neutral view, believing either that AI had no impact on office space demand or that it was too early to determine its effect, according to the property consultancy’s poll of corporate real estate executives in the region.
The remaining 25 per cent said AI adoption would require them to expand their office footprint.
The survey was conducted between May 26 and July 10 across nine markets, including Hong Kong, mainland China, Singapore, Japan, Australia and India. It received 651 responses, with those from the mainland and India weighted more heavily to “reflect those markets’ share of Asia-Pacific grade A office stock”.
The results pointed to AI currently having a more significant impact on office operations than on real estate requirements, CBRE said.
“Although there is speculation that AI could reduce office demand, our findings suggest most organisations remain in the early stages of assessing its impact, with minimal short-term effect on real estate requirements,” said Ada Choi, head of research for Asia-Pacific at CBRE.
“At the same time, many occupiers remain confident in business growth and continue to plan for expansion. As companies rebalance their office portfolio, future growth will be concentrated in higher-quality workplaces, while lower-value space is rationalised.”
What we are seeing now is the emergence of a new equilibrium for the office market
Tom Gaffney, CBRE
AI has been blamed for lay-offs across various sectors, with lower headcounts often linked to reduced office space needs.
Last year, a study by the Switzerland-based World Economic Forum found that 41 per cent of employers across 22 industries in 55 economies planned to reduce their workforce as AI automated certain tasks.
Among CBRE respondents, 46 per cent identified themselves as AI adopters or active movers in applying AI to corporate real estate operations, up from 9 per cent in 2024.
Meanwhile, nearly nine in 10 respondents reported that employees worked in the office at least three days per week, the highest level since the Covid-19 pandemic. Another 85 per cent said office attendance had reached a steady state.
“With attendance and utilisation largely stabilised at higher levels, companies are no longer focused only on bringing employees back to the office,” said Tom Gaffney, head of leasing for Asia-Pacific at CBRE.
“They can now concentrate on transforming the workplace to improve experience and efficiency. What we are seeing now is the emergence of a new equilibrium for the office market, with companies selectively growing their portfolio and prioritising premium workplaces.”

data.title: Hong Kong to recruit AI chief by mid-2027, with confidence in local talent pool
data.description:
Hong Kong will begin recruitment for an artificial intelligence (AI) commissioner in the second quarter of next year to assist in drafting policies for the technology and risk governance, with authorities confident the city does not lack suitable talent.
Tech authorities on Friday revealed details of the new post under the Digital Policy Office, which will pay between HK$262,125 and HK$278,200 (US$33,414 to US$35,436) a month.
Permanent Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Kevin Choi Kit-ming said that recruitment for the post would begin in the second quarter of 2027.
“Their job scope will include providing their expertise and advice on various AI-related activities,” Choi said at a press briefing.
In his policy address on Wednesday, city leader John Lee Ka-chiu said that the commissioner was expected to take up the role next year and would oversee seven key areas of AI risk governance.
These include combating AI-related crimes, such as deepfake porn and online scams, and empowering authorities to remove online content linked to financial fraud.

Choi said the commissioner was also expected to be familiar with developments in the AI industry, including risk governance, global trends, its impact on public administration and its application in local industries.
Choi, who is responsible for the recruitment, said the commissioner would be hired in a recruitment exercise open to both the private and public sectors.
“I deeply believe that the development of AI in Hong Kong is not bad, so we are not worried about a lack of suitable candidates,” he said.
Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan and latest policy address placed a heavy focus on AI as a main driver of the city’s industrial transformation. “Artificial intelligence” appeared more than 190 times in the policy address alone.
Four pages were dedicated to the use of AI across eight industries to boost Hong Kong’s role as an international innovation and technology centre, including taking forward the ‘AI-plus’ initiative, a concept championed by China to integrate the technology into every sector of the economy and society.
Authorities will consult the public on strengthening the legal framework surrounding the technology and improving the detection of AI-generated fraudulent content.
The government will also review whether existing laws adequately address liability for accidents or damage caused by AI products, promote market assessment of ethical risks, step up protection for minors using the technology and ensure they use it with the proper values.
Regarding the timeline for regulating deepfake AI crimes, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok noted that the cybercrime subcommittee under the Law Reform Commission was reviewing the laws, but he was unable to give a “concrete timeline” for the reform.
“Because the [commission] is an independent body comprising members from different industries, it is difficult to state definitively when a final report will be completed,” he said.
However, Lam said he understood public concerns about deepfakes, especially those involving the generation of sexual images or used in fraud. He said he would urge the commission to complete its study as soon as possible.
The new laws would incorporate maximum flexibility to prevent legislation from becoming obsolete as AI technology evolved, he added.
“Many existing laws use technology-neutral language. For example, fraud offences focus on the intent to deceive using tools, regardless of whether those tools are primitive or advanced,” he said.
Flexible “soft laws,” such as industry codes of conduct and public education, could be employed alongside legal measures, Lam added.

data.title: 3 Jellycat, Labubu plushie thieves jailed for up to 2 years and 2 months
data.description:
Three repeat offenders have been sentenced to up to two years and two months behind bars for stealing 83 Jellycat and Labubu plushies worth a total of HK$115,200 (US$14,770) from a Hong Kong shopping centre last year.
The District Court heard on Friday that the three men had stolen the popular merchandise from two claw machine shops at Kwai Chung Plaza on the instructions of other suspects who remain at large.
A waiter, Tang Lik-ming, 35, and a wood painter, Wong Wai-chun, 36, pleaded guilty to two counts of burglary for taking part in the crimes in the early hours of June 9 and June 12 last year.
Part-time warehouse worker Ho Ka-keung, 33, admitted one count of burglary for driving an accomplice to the scene during the second incident.
All three defendants had previous brushes with the law, with Ho and Wong committing the current offences shortly after they were released from prison in 2024 and 2025, respectively.
A prosecution summary of the case said Tang and Wong first met outside the shopping centre at about 3am on June 9.
Carrying four tote bags that Wong gave him, Tang used what appeared to be a stolen key to open a claw machine inside a shop on the second floor and took 23 Jellycat soft toys, each valued at HK$1,000. The two men left the scene separately 10 minutes later.
At about 5am three days later, the pair returned to the shopping centre alongside a wanted suspect to steal 60 Jellycat and Labubu from another shop on the ground floor. The plushies were worth a total of HK$92,200.

Surveillance camera footage revealed that Ho was behind the wheel of a car that took Wong to the shopping centre that morning. Police subsequently seized from the vehicle three tote bags and other items Tang used to commit the offence on June 9.
Under caution, Tang and Wong said they had agreed to take part in the scheme for a reward of up to HK$9,000.
Wong said he recruited Tang to commit the crimes at Ho’s instructions, adding that another wanted suspect had provided the keys to the claw machines to Ho in advance.
Judge Ada Yim Shun-yee said the offences were highly premeditated and all three defendants were aware of their respective roles in the scheme.
She jailed Tang for two years and Ho and Wong for two years and two months each.
Claw machine shops typically operate 24 hours a day, with staff making only occasional visits while relying on CCTV cameras to detect theft.
Burglary is punishable by up to 14 years’ imprisonment in Hong Kong.
The Court of Appeal has set 2½ years’ imprisonment as the customary starting point for sentencing burglary offences outside domestic premises, and three years for offences committed in a domestic setting.

data.title: Doctors urged to test for chikungunya as Hong Kong detects first local 2026 case
data.description:
Doctors in Hong Kong have been urged to arrange blood tests for patients with symptoms of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history, after the city recorded its first local case of the mosquito-borne disease this year.
The Centre for Health Protection issued a reminder to doctors on Thursday after a 55-year-old woman with no recent travel history was reported as Hong Kong’s first locally acquired chikungunya fever case in 2026.
“To facilitate early diagnosis and timely public health intervention, please consider arranging diagnostic testing for any patient presenting with symptoms suggestive of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history,” the centre wrote in a letter to doctors.
Testing for the mosquito-borne disease is free of charge at the public health laboratory service under the centre.
The latest infected woman, who lives on Li Tak Street in Tai Kok Tsui, started to develop symptoms such as fever, headaches and joint pain in her fingers and wrist last Monday, followed by a rash on her face and body.
She sought medical care at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan on Wednesday and was admitted on the same day for treatment. She was in a stable condition.

The woman did not travel during the incubation period, but recalled receiving mosquito bites at her residence and in areas around Cherry Street Park and Lok Kwan Street Park.
The centre is still conducting an epidemiological investigation into the case.
It urged people who had visited Li Tak Street or the two parks and exhibited symptoms such as fever, rash or joint pain to seek medical advice or contact the centre.
The woman is Hong Kong’s third confirmed chikungunya fever case this year. The first two were imported cases reported in January.
Last year, 82 chikungunya cases were recorded in Hong Kong, including 11 local cases.
Mosquito activity, as measured by the government’s Gravidtrap Index, started to pick up in some areas in Hong Kong this month.
In Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun, the initial index for September was 32.1 per cent, falling within the level three readings that indicated the distribution of Aedes albopictus mosquito was “extensive”.
Aedes albopictus is a type of mosquito that can spread diseases such as dengue fever, chikungunya and the Zika virus.
Aberdeen and Ap Lei Chau recorded an index of 26.9 per cent, also reaching the third-highest level in the distribution of mosquitoes under the four-tier system.

data.title: Hong Kong’s metal storage hits 30,000 tonnes in push to become global commodity hub
data.description:
Hong Kong’s push to develop into a premier gold and commodity trading hub has gained momentum, with local metal storage surpassing 30,000 tonnes, a minister has said, as the administration positions the city as the destination of choice for global capital.
Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu also said on Friday the government would expand renminbi settlement of payments for mainland Chinese services, such as buying water from the Dongjiang, in a bid to boost the globalisation of the yuan.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu rolled out an array of measures in his annual policy blueprint on Wednesday to accelerate the growth of the city’s international gold trading market, including a Joint Working Group on Commodity Trading chaired by Hui.
The government will halve the profits tax rate for qualifying physical commodity traders from the standard 16.5 per cent to 8.25 per cent by next year, and the city’s Exchange Fund, used to defend the local currency, will increase its gold portfolio.

The policies followed the launch of the trial operation of Hong Kong’s gold clearing and settlement system in July, which aims to establish the city as a major trading centre and price-setter for the precious metal.
The system is expected to begin operation officially in the first quarter of next year.
Speaking at a press conference, Hui noted total metal storage within Hong Kong’s London Metal Exchange warehouse network had crossed 30,000 tonnes, underscoring the drive to advance commodity trading.
Hong Kong has recorded robust demand for gold imports as banks and logistics companies bet on Hong Kong’s expansion of its vaults for the precious metal.
Data from the Census and Statistics Department showed about 107 tonnes of gold entered Hong Kong in July, up from 72.16 tonnes in February.
Hui noted that the trial operation of the gold clearing system had proceeded smoothly, attracting substantial deposits.
Beyond the 11 banks taking part in the trial, authorities received inquiries from other institutions interested in joining the gold trading ecosystem, which Hui described as a “good sign”.
On government payments, the policy address proposed expanding yuan payments for services rendered by mainland authorities.
Hui said the arrangements were already in place on a limited scale and described the increase as a natural next step.
He added that officials were considering paying in yuan for Dongjiang water supplies – which account for up to 80 per cent of the city’s fresh water from the Taiyuan Pumping Station in Dongguan city – as well as for training programmes run by mainland institutions.
At the same press conference, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah revealed that authorities were liaising with more than 40 companies interested in establishing a presence in the Northern Metropolis.
“Many of them are in innovation and technology, including hydrogen energy [and] new energy development, and the other one is in quantum science, and we got another one building a logistics park,” Yau said.
To attract enterprises to the 30,000-hectare (74,130-acre) megaproject, which will feature several innovation hubs and university clusters, the government is offering tailored incentive packages featuring land-use facilitation, co-investment options and tax breaks based on operation scale.
